text: Cloth is what the three parts of this film have in common, and little else. Jia Zhangke sets a large production line, a designer readying a hand-made collection called Wuyong for Paris Fashion Week, and the shrinking trade of tailors in the small town of Fengdang beside one another and lets the distances show. The factory measures output; the atelier measures intention; in Fengdang the measuring is done on a customer standing still. Eighty-four minutes is short for that much country. The attention goes to hands rather than to opinions: measuring, cutting, waiting for work that used to arrive. Its ordering is the argument, and the argument is that everything worn somewhere was made somewhere else, by someone the wearer will not meet.

Two people married to other people meet in a blue hotel room and plan a future neither can actually arrange. Mathieu Amalric takes seventy-six minutes over it, less than most thrillers spend on a first act, and the compression is the method. Crime, romance, thriller: the labels are all on the file, and the film declines to keep them separate. An affair remembered fondly is also a timeline, and a timeline is what an inquiry wants. So the pleasures come back in a flatter voice, with dates attached, and an afternoon that felt like escape starts to sound like arrangement. Whether there was a crime at all stays open for a long while. The blue is the kind of detail a lover keeps and an investigator writes down.

Thirty years of near misses teach a crowd a particular way of talking about its own team, cautious in the manner of people discussing weather. James Erskine had the run of Liverpool Football Club for a season, and the film's interest is less in matches than in the conditions around them: training-ground routine, the arithmetic supporters do in their heads, the distance between a stadium in one city and a living room several time zones from it. Ninety-nine minutes, much of it indoors. Football documentaries with this level of access usually spend it on tactics. This one spends a good deal of it on people who have been waiting, and on what a season looks like from inside a club that knows exactly how long the wait has been.

The wagon in this Western is pointed east. Three women on the Nebraska frontier have been broken by what living there asks of them, and the work of delivering them to a minister and his wife in Iowa falls to Mary Bee Cuddy: pious, capable, and short of help. She hires a drifter named George Briggs to come along. What follows is two hours of open country in which the threat is partly weather and partly the cargo, since derangement inside a covered wagon is not something a rifle can be aimed at. The genre's usual arrangement gets reversed: the woman holds the plan, the hired man is the liability, and the damage done by frontier life is transported rather than avenged. The country stays beautiful the whole way, which is part of the discomfort.

Before it can be a battle, Sekigahara has to be a ledger of promises: who has pledged what to whom, and what a pledge is worth breaking for. Masato Harada spends 150 minutes on the 1600 confrontation between Tokugawa Ieyasu's Army of the East and Ishida Mitsunari's Army of the West, and much of that time goes to retainers, in-laws and household calculation rather than to cavalry. That is the harder film to make. A war picture aimed at an audience that already knows the names can use the foreknowledge as pressure: every courtesy between commanders is also a man working out how long to keep his word. The fighting, when it arrives, has the character of accounting, with sums coming due on agreements made months earlier in rooms.

Karen gave up a daughter as a teenager and has spent the decades since arranging her life around that fact. Rodrigo García keeps three households apart for a long stretch: Karen; Elizabeth, a lawyer who was adopted herself and holds everyone at a measured distance; and Lucy, who cannot conceive and is now in the position of hoping to be chosen by a stranger. Adoption here is largely procedure, interviews and agencies and the particular politeness of adults being assessed as suitable, and the film trusts that to be dramatic enough. It took the Grand prix du Festival de Deauville, a good fit for something that advances at conversation length rather than by incident. Two hours insisting that the arrangement involved three people, and that none of them were asked the same question.

The Kerrigan house stands a few yards from the runways at Tullamarine, and the family regards this as a feature. Rob Sitch's comedy gives eighty-five minutes to a compulsory acquisition: an inspector condemns the place, the government wants the land for airport expansion, and Darryl Kerrigan declines to accept that a valuation describes anything he owns. His lawyer, Dennis Denuto, is out of his depth, and the film is fond of him for it. An AACTA Award for a leading role came out of this, a reasonable outcome for a performance built almost entirely on sincerity. The jokes run on taste: the extensions, the pergola, the pride taken in features a catalogue would call improvements. None of them are aimed at the people who love the house.

Snow begins over Seoul, and two men who used to be close sit down to eat and drink, which in Hong Sang-soo is a form of excavation. One of them teaches at a college; the other has come back from the United States with a film career that failed to happen. Eighty-eight minutes, most of them at tables, and at some point they decide to go and find a young woman they each once wanted, as though she were something left in storage. The reminiscing is the substance, and what the men present as devotion does not always sound that way once it is spoken aloud. Nothing is confronted. The glasses are refilled, the snow keeps up, and the search proceeds at the pace of two men in no particular hurry to arrive anywhere.
